![The Directions a Matrix Refuses to Turn](./cover.png)

A matrix does two things to a vector: it turns it and stretches it. Feed in
almost any direction and you get both. But most matrices have a few directions
that come back pointing *exactly where they started*, just longer or shorter.
Those are the **eigenvectors**, and the stretch is the **eigenvalue**.

## Every matrix has a few directions it only stretches

$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ is made up, not measured —
one step of a two-group population model. These four whole numbers give
eigenvalues of exactly 5 and 2, keeping the arithmetic out of the way. A real
one would have hundreds of dimensions and messy decimal eigenvalues, which you
could not draw — and drawing it is the point. Also, $A$ is not symmetric — that
matters shortly.

`numpy.linalg.eig` hands you both at once:

::: {#5c098a77 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

A = np.array([[4.0, 1.0], [2.0, 3.0]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)

# numpy 2.x returns complex dtype from eig even when every eigenvalue is real,
# as they are here. It also returns unit-length eigenvectors; since these are
# defined only up to scale, rescale each to start with a 1 so the whole numbers
# below match the text. (Fine here -- a zero first entry would need another
# pivot, and a rotation matrix has no real eigenvector to rescale at all.)
vals, vecs = vals.real, vecs.real
vecs = vecs / vecs[0]

for lam, v in zip(vals, vecs.T):
    print(f"lambda = {lam:5.2f}   eigenvector = {v}   A @ v = {A @ v}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
lambda =  5.00   eigenvector = [1. 1.]   A @ v = [5. 5.]
lambda =  2.00   eigenvector = [ 1. -2.]   A @ v = [ 2. -4.]
```
:::
:::


Both do what they promise: `A @ v` is `v` with every number multiplied by the
same amount.

## $A = PDP^{-1}$ is that idea written as a formula

Put the eigenvectors in the columns of $P$, their eigenvalues down the diagonal
of $D$, and you can rebuild the matrix:

$$A = PDP^{-1}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 & v_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D =
\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Read it right to left: $P^{-1}$ redescribes a vector in eigenvector terms, $D$
stretches each part by its own eigenvalue, and $P$ converts back. The eigenvalues come from the characteristic equation
$\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$, here $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0$.

Multiplying the three back together gives $A$. Drawing the map on a circle of
unit vectors shows why the eigenvectors are special:

::: {#af43a403 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ACCENT = "#4A3AA7"
GREY = "#999999"

P = vecs
D = np.diag(vals)
print(f"max |A - P D P^-1| = {np.abs(A - P @ D @ np.linalg.inv(P)).max():.2e}")

theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
circle = np.vstack([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])
image = A @ circle

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 6.2))
ax.axhline(0, color="0.85", lw=1, zorder=0)
ax.axvline(0, color="0.85", lw=1, zorder=0)
ax.plot(*circle, color=GREY, lw=1.3, label="unit circle")
ax.plot(*image, color="#444444", lw=1.6, label="image under $A$")

for k, (lam, v) in enumerate(zip(vals, vecs.T)):
    u = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
    ax.annotate(
        "",
        xy=lam * u,
        xytext=(0, 0),
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=ACCENT, lw=2.2, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0),
        zorder=3,
    )
    # Mark where the eigenvector meets the unit circle: the arrow is that same
    # point scaled by lambda, and its tip lands back on the ellipse.
    ax.plot(*u, marker="o", ms=6, color="white", mec=ACCENT, mew=1.8, zorder=5)
    ax.plot([], [], color=ACCENT, lw=2.2, label=f"eigenvector, $\\lambda = {lam:.0f}$")
    ax.annotate(
        f"$\\lambda_{k + 1} = {lam:.0f}$",
        xy=lam * u,
        xytext=(16, 12 * np.sign(u[1])),
        textcoords="offset points",
        color=ACCENT,
        fontsize=11,
        va="center",
    )

ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(-6, 6)
ax.set_ylim(-6, 6)
ax.grid(False)
for side in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=10)
ax.set_title("Dots: unit eigenvectors on the circle. Arrows: their images under $A$.",
             fontsize=10, color="0.3")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
max |A - P D P^-1| = 8.88e-16
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-2.png){}
:::
:::


The circle becomes an ellipse, and the purple arrows land near its long and
short axes but not on them. That near miss is real, not a bug: those axes belong
to $A$'s *singular* vectors, which match the eigenvectors only for a symmetric
matrix.

## Diagonal matrices turn repeated work into simple arithmetic

The payoff comes when you apply $A$ repeatedly. Each inner $P^{-1}P$ cancels,
leaving $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$ — raising a matrix to the hundredth power becomes
raising two *numbers* to that power, and the bigger eigenvalue soon takes over.
That is why it appears wherever a map runs again and again.

| Concept | What it is | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| Eigenvector | a direction $v$ with $Av = \lambda v$ | PCA's principal axes |
| Eigenvalue | the scale factor $\lambda$ along $v$ | variance explained |
| Characteristic equation | $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ | finding the spectrum |
| Decomposition | $A = PDP^{-1}$ | Markov chain steady states |
| When it exists | $n$ independent eigenvectors (diagonalizable) | vibration normal modes |

So the directions a matrix refuses to turn give you the viewpoint where it stops
being a matrix and becomes a short list of numbers. It breaks for a rotation,
which turns every direction and has no real eigenvector at all, and for
defective matrices, which lack the independent eigenvectors to fill $P$. And
since this $A$ is not symmetric, its eigenvectors are not at right angles, so
$P^{-1} \neq P^{\top}$ and the switch can go numerically wobbly — the reason
[Matrix Factorizations as Optimization Problems](../matrix-factorizations/)
reaches for the SVD instead.
